Leap days are needed to keep our calendar in alignment with the Earth's revolutions around the Sun. It takes the Earth approximately 365.242189 days—or 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes, and 45 seconds—to circle once around the Sun. This is called a tropical year. Without an extra, or intercalary day on February 29 nearly every four years, we would lose almost six hours every year.

After only 100 years, a calendar without leap years would be off by approximately 24 days. Seasonal days such as the vernal equinox or the winter solstice would, therefore, shift in relation to the months in the calendar. For example, in 100 years, the Northern Hemisphere's autumnal equinox, which falls in late September, would fall in late August, and in a few centuries, August would become a spring month. extra_snippets: The next leap year is 2028, and leap day falls on Tuesday, February 29, 2028. The rule is simple in one breath and tricky in the fine print: a year is a leap year if it divides evenly by 4, with one exception for century years.

A common (non-leap) year is exactly 52 weeks plus one day. That extra day is the reason a birthday that lands on a Tuesday in one common year lands on a Wednesday the next. A leap year, by contrast, is 52 weeks plus two days. If your birthday fell on a Wednesday last year, in a leap year it “leaps” past Thursday and lands on Friday.

The exception inside the exception is the part that trips people up. In practice it means a small handful of century years that look like leap years on the four-rule are not. The years 1700, 1800, and 1900 were not leap years; they divide by 4 but they also divide by 100 without dividing by 400. The year 2000 was a leap year; it divides by 400, so the second exception turned it back into a leap year. The next century year to skip leap day is 2100, then 2200, then 2300.

The next one to keep it is 2400. That double exception is not a quirk; it is what makes the calendar accurate. The plain four-year rule overshoots by about 11 minutes a year, so the century-year correction trims about three days every 400 years. The math works out to an average year length of 365.2425 days, which is within roughly 26 seconds of the true solar year. Leap day is an artifact that dates back to 46 BC, when Julius Caesar took the advice of the learned astronomer Sosigenes of Alexandria.

Note: The above rule does not apply to century years. Centuries such as 1900 and 2000 only have a leap day if they are divisible by 400. 1900 is divisible by 4 and also by 100, but not by 400, so not a leap year. This means that centuries are only a leap year if they are divisible by 400.
